title: Extradural (epidural) haematoma
scenario: CT brain shown (archive file, two separate cases). Archive
Trauma manikin: 25-year-old RTA patient, unconscious; after ABCD "the patient has a unilateral fixed dilated pupil" → CT head shown. 430A
CT picture station. 437A · 438F · 439B
Unmanned station — CT picture. 441A

imgs.cap: CT head — biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection with midline shift CT head — large extradural haematoma
441A exam CT — left extradural haematoma CT head — right extradural haematoma (437A, "mention the side")
CT head — right parietal extradural haematoma (430A)

qs.q: What is the radiological finding? / Mention 2 findings.
a: Peripheral hyperdense, biconvex (lens-shaped) extra-axial collection limited by the sutures, with mass effect / midline shift and compressed lateral ventricle. Mention the side.
qs.why: Fresh blood is hyperdense on CT; a biconvex collection that doesn't cross sutures is extradural, and mass effect (midline shift, compressed ventricle) shows how dangerous it is. Always say the side.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Extradural (epidural) haematoma.
qs.why: A lens-shaped extra-axial hyperdensity after head trauma = extradural haematoma.

qs.q: Why does it take this shape?
a: The dura is firmly attached at the sutures, so the blood is limited between them (e.g. coronal & lambdoid) → lens shape.
qs.why: Arterial blood strips the dura off the skull but is stopped where the dura is tightly fixed at the sutures — so it bulges inwards as a lens.

qs.q: What is the type of herniation?
a: Answer given: cingulate (sub-falcine) — the midline shift seen on CT; uncal (transtentorial) herniation causes the dilated pupil.
qs.why: The midline shift on CT is the brain pushed under the falx (subfalcine/cingulate herniation); the dilated pupil comes from the uncus herniating through the tentorium onto CN III.

qs.q: What is lateralisation?
a: Ipsilateral dilated pupil + contralateral hemiparesis.
qs.why: The expanding clot compresses the ipsilateral CN III (dilated pupil) and the cerebral peduncle, whose fibres cross below — so weakness is on the opposite side.

qs.q: What is the lucid interval?
a: A period of consciousness between two periods of unconsciousness: first loss from concussion → wakes → deteriorates after hours as the haematoma expands and compresses the brainstem (RAS).
qs.why: Initial concussion causes brief loss of consciousness; the patient recovers while the arterial clot slowly enlarges, then deteriorates as it compresses the brain — the classic EDH story.

qs.q: What is the source of bleeding?
a: Middle meningeal artery.
qs.why: A temporal (pterion) fracture tears the middle meningeal artery — arterial bleeding explains the rapid expansion.

qs.q: The patient has a unilateral fixed dilated pupil — what will you do?
a: Urgent non-contrast CT head.
qs.why: A blown pupil means herniation from a mass lesion — urgent CT finds the haematoma for immediate evacuation.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: In the ER: ABCD — protect the airway, oxygenate (> 95 %), maintain circulation (CPP = MAP − ICP: raise MAP, lower ICP); calculate GCS; call the neurosurgeon.
Definitive: craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma.
qs.why: Prevent secondary brain injury (hypoxia, hypotension, high ICP) and evacuate the clot by craniotomy — EDH has an excellent outcome when operated early.

qs.q: How do you lower raised ICP (and how does each measure help)?
a: Head elevation 30–45° (venous drainage), mannitol / hypertonic saline (osmotic), controlled hyperventilation (vasoconstriction — fastest, temporary), sedation, loading dose of phenytoin (seizure prophylaxis), ICP monitoring, treat the cause.
qs.why: ICP falls by improving venous drainage, drawing water out of the brain osmotically, and vasoconstricting cerebral vessels (hyperventilation, briefly); preventing seizures avoids ICP spikes.

extra.q: How to read a head CT for haematoma
a: Lens shape → extradural (no chronic EDH). Crescent → subdural: hyperdense = acute, isodense = subacute, hypodense = chronic. Compare density with brain (bone most dense, air least).
Raise MAP: 2 large-bore lines with pressure bags, inotropes, blood, stop bleeding. Presentation: lateralising signs, ↓LOC, ± Cushing's triad.

title: Ring-enhancing brain lesion — tumour / metastases / abscess
scenario: CT/MRI brain with a ring-enhancing lesion in the occipital lobe (427 file). 427
MRI — ring-enhancing lesion in the left hemisphere. Archive
Neuro-tumour station (similar picture). 435
Axial CT brain — bilateral heterogeneous, well-circumscribed masses with oedema in the frontal and parietal lobes. 439A · 442B

imgs.cap: T1 post-contrast MRI — ring-enhancing occipital lesion T1 post-contrast MRI — ring-enhancing lesion, left hemisphere
T1 post-contrast MRI — ring-enhancing lesion (second archive case)
CT — bilateral ring-enhancing masses with surrounding oedema (439A & 442B)

qs.q: Describe what you see in detail. / Read the image.
a: Axial T1 MRI with contrast (or contrast CT): intra-axial lesion with ring (rim) enhancement and surrounding hypodense oedema — name the lobe and side (439A/442B: bilateral frontal & parietal).
qs.why: Describe modality and sequence, location (lobe and side), the ring enhancement and the surrounding oedema.

qs.q: Where is the lesion?
a: Left cerebral hemisphere.
qs.why: Name the hemisphere (and lobe) — localisation explains the symptoms.

qs.q: What is the differential diagnosis?
a: MAGIC DR: Metastasis, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct (subacute), Contusion, Demyelination (tumefactive MS), Radiation necrosis.
4 common: metastasis, glioma (GBM), abscess, lymphoma (also TB, sarcoidosis; pituitary adenoma/meningioma in 435's list).
qs.why: Ring enhancement is non-specific: metastasis, abscess and glioblastoma are the commonest; MAGIC DR lists the rest.

qs.q: What are the signs and symptoms? / signs of raised ICP?
a: Occipital: visual changes — homonymous hemianopia.
Focal: seizures, focal deficits.
Raised ICP: headache, nausea/vomiting, papilloedema (blurred vision), ↓ level of
consciousness.
qs.why: Symptoms come from the lobe involved (occipital → visual field loss), from irritation (seizures), and from raised ICP (headache, vomiting, papilloedema).

qs.q: What questions would you ask in the history?
a: Differentiate the causes: metastasis (known cancer? breast/colon/lung symptoms, smoking, screening), lymphoma (B symptoms), infection (fever, recent infection, TB contact, travel, immunosuppression/HIV, IV drugs), GBM (only neurological symptoms).
qs.why: The history separates the causes: known cancer (metastasis), fever/immunosuppression (abscess, TB), B symptoms (lymphoma), purely neurological (GBM).
hist: Known cancer, breast/colon/lung symptoms, smoking, screening
Metastasis is the commonest cause of multiple ring-enhancing lesions in adults.
B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
Fever, recent infection, TB contact, travel
Suggest an abscess or infective cause (TB, parasites).
Toxoplasmosis, lymphoma and abscess are commoner in the immunocompromised.
A primary tumour (GBM) presents with neurological features alone.

qs.q: What investigations would you do?
a: MRI brain with contrast (diagnostic test).
Labs: CBC, coagulation, serology; TB work-up (culture, tuberculin, PCR); look for a primary: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, bone scan, PET — know why you order each (support your DDx).
qs.why: MRI with contrast characterises the lesion; body imaging finds a primary; infection work-up if abscess is possible.

qs.q: What is the most common primary brain tumour?
a: Glioblastoma (GBM).
qs.why: Glioblastoma is the commonest primary malignant brain tumour in adults (metastases are commoner overall).

qs.q: What is the management?
a: ABC, call the neurosurgeon, reduce oedema/ICP (mannitol, dexamethasone), surgery (resection/biopsy) ± oncological treatment.
qs.why: Control ICP and oedema first; tissue diagnosis and debulking by surgery guide oncological therapy.

qs.q: What is the hypodense area around each mass, and how do you manage it?
a: Vasogenic oedema → steroids (dexamethasone).
qs.why: The leaky tumour vessels cause vasogenic oedema, which responds to dexamethasone.

title: Acute subdural haematoma
scenario: A 33-year-old man in an MVA: opens eyes to pain, inappropriate sounds, abnormal (spastic) flexion to pain (other group: withdraws from pain); urgent CT shown. Archive
A 20-year-old RTA patient: hypotensive, HR 130, SpO₂ 90 %; eyes open to pain, withdraws from pain, incomprehensible sounds; pupils 3 mm and 5 mm — CT: acute SDH with midline shift. 441F
Unmanned CT station. 441A
CT station — "right-sided acute subdural haematoma". 437A
Patient confused, opens eyes to pain, withdraws from pain — CT shown. 442F

imgs.cap: CT head — crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines (441A & 442F exam image)
CT head — acute subdural haematoma with midline shift

qs.q: Calculate his GCS.
a: Eyes to pain 2 + inappropriate/incomprehensible sounds 2 + abnormal flexion 3 = 7 (ARC1). 441F: E2 + V2 + M4 = 8. 442F: E2 + V4 (confused) + M4 = 10.
qs.why: Score the best response in each category: eyes, verbal, motor — the total grades severity and decides intubation (≤ 8).

qs.q: Describe the CT / mention the findings.
a: Crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the brain surface, crossing suture lines, with midline shift (sub-falcine herniation) and effacement of the ventricle/sulci.
qs.why: A crescent along the convexity that crosses sutures is subdural; mass effect is described as midline shift and ventricular effacement.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Acute subdural haematoma (mention the side).
qs.why: A crescentic hyperdense collection crossing sutures in a head-injured patient = acute subdural haematoma.

qs.q: What is the (main) source of bleeding?
a: Bridging (cortical) veins.
qs.why: Acceleration–deceleration tears the bridging veins crossing the subdural space — venous blood spreads widely along the brain.

qs.q: What is the management? (5 steps)
a: A: secure airway — endotracheal intubation (GCS ≤ 8); B: if intubated but not breathing → mechanical ventilation; C: 2 large-bore IV lines, bloods & cross-match, IV fluids/blood; D: GCS, pupils; call the neurosurgeon.
qs.why: GCS ≤ 8 can't protect the airway; hypoxia and hypotension double mortality in head injury, so ABC comes first, then neurosurgery.

qs.q: How do you lower the ICP?
a: Mannitol / hypertonic saline, head of bed 30–45°, controlled hyperventilation, sedation, avoid hypotension/hypoxia.
qs.why: Reducing ICP preserves cerebral perfusion (CPP = MAP − ICP) while preparing for surgery.

qs.q: What is the definitive treatment?
a: Craniotomy (decompressive) and evacuation of the haematoma.
qs.why: A significant acute SDH with mass effect needs craniotomy to evacuate the clot and relieve pressure.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
scenario: A 32-year-old woman presents to the ER with a sudden "worst headache of her life"; now stable, GCS 15/15. (new case) 442A
CT picture stations. 437A · 441A · Archive

imgs.cap: Non-contrast CT — subarachnoid haemorrhage (basal cisterns) Cerebral angiogram — saccular aneurysm
CT — blood in the basal cisterns (arrow) CT — diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage (441A)

qs.q: What imaging modalities would you order?
a: Non-contrast CT brain (± LP if CT negative), CT angiography / MRI, digital subtraction angiography (DSA).
qs.why: Non-contrast CT is very sensitive in the first hours; LP (xanthochromia) if CT is negative; CTA/DSA find the aneurysm.

qs.q: What is the radiological finding / diagnosis?
a: Hyperdense (white) blood in the subarachnoid spaces/basal cisterns where CSF (black) should be → subarachnoid haemorrhage.
qs.why: Blood is white on CT, so blood in the cisterns/sulci where black CSF should be = SAH.

qs.q: What is the most common cause, and the most common non-traumatic cause?
a: Most common overall: trauma. Most common non-traumatic (spontaneous): ruptured (berry) aneurysm.
qs.why: Trauma is the commonest cause of subarachnoid blood overall; spontaneous SAH is usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

qs.q: What are other causes?
a: AV malformation, trauma, (dissection, vasculitis, coagulopathy).
qs.why: AVMs and other vascular lesions cause the remainder of spontaneous SAH.

qs.q: What are the management options?
a: ABCD, call the neurosurgeon, nimodipine, BP control.
Secure the aneurysm: surgical clipping or endovascular coiling (stent-assisted if wide neck).
qs.why: Nimodipine reduces vasospasm-related ischaemia; the aneurysm must be secured (clip or coil) early to prevent re-bleeding, which is often fatal.

tips.t: 442A — the doctor said don't say stenting.

a: Coiling avoids open surgery but is expensive, may recanalise, and coils can migrate (stroke) → needs angiographic follow-up.

title: Meningioma
scenario: Post-contrast MRI shown in the neuro picture station (remember to mention the side). 437A

imgs.cap: Post-contrast MRI — extra-axial, homogeneously enhancing mass (right)

qs.q: Mention 2 features.
a: Extra-axial (dural-based, broad attachment ± dural tail), homogeneous enhancement.
qs.why: Meningiomas arise from the dura — extra-axial with a broad dural base, dural tail and bright homogeneous enhancement.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Meningioma (right side).
qs.why: An extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneously enhancing mass = meningioma (say the side).

title: Spinal cord compression — lung-cancer metastases (lower- limb exam)
scenario: A patient with lung cancer presents with inability to walk and loss of sensation in the lower limbs — examine the motor & sensory system of the lower limbs (simulated patient: sensory level at T10 / below the umbilicus, decreased power in both legs). 430F · Old exam

qs.q: Examine the motor and sensory system of the lower limbs.
a: Tone, power, reflexes, plantars, clonus, all sensory modalities — establish the sensory level (T10 = umbilicus).
qs.why: Establishing UMN weakness and a sensory level confirms cord compression and localises it.

qs.q: What would you like to ask the patient based on your findings?
a: Faecal and urinary continence (sphincter involvement).
qs.why: Bladder and bowel involvement means advanced compression — an emergency, and it affects prognosis.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Metastases to the spine with spinal cord compression.
qs.why: A cancer patient with new leg weakness and a sensory level has metastatic cord compression until proven otherwise.

qs.q: What investigation would you like to do?
a: Urgent MRI of the whole spine.
qs.why: Urgent whole-spine MRI shows the level(s) of compression (often multiple) — treatment (steroids, radiotherapy/surgery) must start within hours.

title: Pituitary adenoma
scenario: Coronal MRI of the sella. Archive

imgs.cap: Coronal post-contrast MRI — sellar/suprasellar mass (similar picture)

qs.q: What is your most likely diagnosis?
a: Pituitary adenoma.
qs.why: A sellar mass on coronal MRI is a pituitary adenoma until proven otherwise.

qs.q: What further investigations would you order?
a: Hormonal assay: prolactin, GH/IGF-1, ACTH/cortisol, FSH/LH, TSH/T4; formal visual fields.
qs.why: Adenomas may secrete hormones or cause hypopituitarism (hormone panel), and press on the optic chiasm (visual fields — bitemporal hemianopia).

qs.q: Name two surgical approaches.
a: Extracranial: transsphenoidal (endoscopic endonasal or microscopic). Transcranial: subfrontal, subtemporal, pterional.
qs.why: Most are removed through the nose and sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal); large suprasellar tumours may need a craniotomy.

qs.q: Name 5 complications of surgery.
a: Diabetes insipidus, CSF rhinorrhoea, meningitis, pituitary apoplexy/haemorrhage,
hypopituitarism, visual/nerve damage.
qs.why: Surgery near the stalk/posterior pituitary causes DI; opening the sella risks CSF leak and meningitis; damage to the gland causes hypopituitarism; the optic apparatus can be injured.

title: Base-of-skull fracture
scenario: Skull-base fracture station (427). No questions were written down — know the signs. 427

qs.q: What are the signs of a base-of-skull fracture? (questions not recorded)
a: Raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), Battle's sign (mastoid bruising), CSF
rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea, haemotympanum, cranial-nerve palsies (VII, VIII).
qs.why: Blood and CSF track from the fractured skull base into the orbits and mastoid; a torn dura leaks CSF from nose or ear; the petrous bone carries CN VII and VIII.

title: Spinal cord injury — Brown-Séquard (stab wound)
scenario: A man presented to the ER with a stab wound in the back. On exam: hypertonia and decreased power in the left lower limb, loss of pain/temperature sensation on the right up to the nipple line (T4) with intact proprioception (other group: T7 — "where is T7?"). Archive

qs.q: Perform a lower-limb motor and sensory examination.
a: Inspection, tone, power (MRC grades), reflexes, plantar response, clonus; sensation (light touch, pin-prick, temperature, vibration, proprioception) — find the sensory level.
qs.why: A full lower-limb examination finds the pattern (UMN signs) and the sensory level, which localises a cord lesion.

qs.q: What is the grade of power? (know the grades well)
a: MRC: 0 none · 1 flicker · 2 movement with gravity eliminated · 3 against gravity · 4 against some resistance · 5 normal.
qs.why: MRC grading is the standard way to record power.

qs.q: Name the lesion. / What is the name of this syndrome?
a: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of the cord): ipsilateral weakness + loss of
proprioception/vibration; contralateral loss of pain & temperature.
qs.why: A hemisection cuts the corticospinal tract and dorsal columns on the same side (ipsilateral weakness, loss of proprioception) and the already-crossed spinothalamic tract (contralateral pain/temperature loss).

qs.q: Where is the lesion?
a: Thoracic spinal cord (≈ T4 at the nipple line; T6 = xiphisternum, T7 just below it).
qs.why: The sensory level localises the lesion: nipple line = T4, umbilicus = T10.

qs.q: What are the complications after this type of injury?
a: Bleeding, infection (CSF leak/meningitis), progression of cord injury, peripheral nerve injury.
qs.why: A penetrating cord wound risks bleeding, CSF leak/meningitis and further cord damage.

qs.q: How will you manage this case?
a: ABCD, wound care, (leave a retained blade in situ), tetanus, CT/MRI, call the neurosurgeon.
qs.why: Trauma priorities first; never pull out a retained blade (it may tamponade a vessel) — image and remove in theatre with neurosurgery.

title: Motor examination — hemiparesis
scenario: A patient with headache, right-sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. Archive

qs.q: Examine the motor system and reflexes of the upper and lower limbs.
a: Inspection (wasting, fasciculation), tone, power (MRC), reflexes (biceps, triceps, supinator, knee, ankle), plantars, coordination — expect UMN signs on the right.
qs.why: Headache + hemiparesis + dysphasia suggests a left hemisphere lesion; examining tone, power, reflexes and plantars confirms an upper motor neurone pattern on the right.

title: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
scenario: A 50-year-old man with 6 months of unsteady gait, bilateral hand numbness and difficulty with fine motor tasks. (new case) 442F

qs.q: What are the key clinical findings?
a: Gait disturbance (difficult tandem walking), loss of fine motor skills (clumsy hands), bilateral symptoms, increased tone in upper & lower limbs (spasticity).
qs.why: Cord compression in the neck causes UMN signs in the legs (spastic gait) and myelopathic hands (clumsiness, numbness), usually bilaterally.

qs.q: What do you suspect?
a: Cervical myelopathy (spinal cord compression).
qs.why: Bilateral hand clumsiness with gait disturbance and spasticity in a middle-aged man = cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

qs.q: What is the sign being tested in the picture?
a: Hoffmann's sign.
qs.why: Flicking the middle finger nail and watching the thumb tests for Hoffmann's sign.

qs.q: What is Hoffmann's sign and how is it performed?
a: A test of upper-motor-neurone dysfunction: flick the distal phalanx (nail) of the middle finger downward; positive = involuntary flexion of the thumb and index finger.
qs.why: Flicking the distal phalanx stretches the finger flexors; with an UMN lesion the exaggerated reflex makes the thumb and index flex.

qs.q: What does a positive Hoffmann's sign indicate?
a: Upper motor neurone lesion — suggests cervical cord compression.
qs.why: It is the upper-limb equivalent of a hyperreflexic sign — pointing to cervical cord compression.

qs.q: What investigation will you order?
a: MRI cervical spine (gold standard).
qs.why: MRI shows the cord, the level and degree of compression, and cord signal change.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Surgical decompression (definitive).
qs.why: Myelopathy is progressive; decompression stops further deterioration.
